author: camjac251
body:
## Summary

Adds the VoyageAI `voyage-4` series (`voyage-code-4`, `voyage-4`, `voyage-4-large`, `voyage-4-lite`) to `VOYAGE_MODEL_CONFIG`, and makes an existing index keep the embedding model it was built with.

[`voyage-code-4`](https://blog.voyageai.com/2026/08/13/voyage-code-4/) launched 2026-08-13. It is trained on queries mined from issue-fixing pull requests rather than on source paired with docstrings, which targets retrieval from a symptom description rather than from a known identifier. Voyage reports it ahead of `voyage-code-3` by 27.54% on their agentic code-retrieval benchmark and by 13.98% across the 28 datasets used to evaluate `voyage-code-3`, at $0.12 per 1M tokens against `voyage-code-3`'s $0.18. Their [FAQ](https://docs.voyageai.com/docs/faq) now lists it as the recommended model for code.

**The default stays `voyage-3.5`.** An earlier revision of this PR moved it and @grzegorznowak was right to block that; the reasoning is in [Model changes](#model-changes) below.

None of the 4 series was in `VOYAGE_MODEL_CONFIG`, so all four resolved to `DEFAULT_UNKNOWN_MODEL_CONFIG`:

- `voyage-4-large` was batched against a 320K token budget when the API enforces 120K, so large batches failed with `TOO_MANY_TOKENS_IN_BATCH`.
- `voyage-4-lite` was capped at 320K against a 1M limit.
- The fallback carries an empty `dimensions` list, so an unsupported `output_dims` was accepted at construction and only rejected by the API mid-index.

## Model changes

The review raised that changing the default risks a silent full re-embed for anyone who never set `embedding.model`, and that an interrupted switch leaves duplicate model-tagged vectors per chunk. Both hold. `_get_chunks_without_embeddings(provider, model)` re-embeds every chunk lacking a row for the new model and never removes the old rows.

There is a third consequence worth naming: `SearchService` filters stored vectors by `(provider, model)`, so between the switch and the end of the re-embed, semantic search returns **nothing at all**.

So this reverts the default, and also removes the underlying footgun rather than just this instance of it. Once a database holds embeddings under a `(provider, model)` pair, that pair is sticky and configuration becomes a proposal:

| Context | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `chunkhound index` at a terminal | Warns, reports how many chunks a switch would rewrite, asks. Declining keeps the indexed model, leaves search working, asks again next run. |
| Non-interactive / `CHUNKHOUND_NO_PROMPTS=1` | Warns, keeps the indexed model, re-embeds nothing. |
| MCP startup | Keeps the indexed model, reason logged to stderr. No decision hook is constructed, so nothing reaches stdout. |
| Configured *provider* differs | Applied as configured. Credentials and dimensions leave nothing to fall back to. |

The pin is written back to `config.embedding.model` as well as the live provider. `search` and `create_services` build their own provider straight from `config.embedding` rather than asking the registry; pinning only the registry instance left those querying a model the index does not hold, which reproduced the empty-result bug this is meant to prevent. There is a regression test for exactly that.

This also makes a future default change safe: an existing index would keep `voyage-3.5` and be offered the switch, while new indexes start on the newer model. Happy to revisit moving the default in a follow-up once this has settled.

## Suggestion layer

Per the review's proposal, when a newer model supersedes the one in use, `chunkhound index` prints one informational line stating what switching costs, and never acts on it:

```text
[INFO] voyage-code-4 supersedes voyage-code-3. Switching re-embeds every chunk
       and leaves the voyage-code-3 vectors in place until removed, so it is not
       automatic: set embedding.model to voyage-code-4 when you want it.
       Silence this with CHUNKHOUND_NO_MODEL_SUGGESTIONS=1.
```

Upgrade targets stay in-family (`voyage-3.5` to `voyage-4`, `voyage-3.5-lite` to `voyage-4-lite`, `voyage-3-large` to `voyage-4-large`); only the code model points at the code-specialised successor.

## Model configuration

Four new entries sharing a 32K context window, 1,000 texts per batch, `dimensions` `[256, 512, 1024, 2048]`, and a 1024 default. Per-batch token limits differ:

| Model | Tokens per batch |
|---|---|
| `voyage-code-4` | 320,000 |
| `voyage-4` | 320,000 |
| `voyage-4-large` | 120,000 |
| `voyage-4-lite` | 1,000,000 |

Limits were measured against the live API rather than taken from the docs, which omit `voyage-code-4` from the `output_dimension` and per-batch token lists in both the [API reference](https://docs.voyageai.com/reference/embeddings-api) and the [embeddings guide](https://docs.voyageai.com/docs/embeddings). The API states each limit in its rejection message. `voyage-code-3` was probed as a control and returned the 120K already in the table.

## Verification

- Real index: built on `voyage-code-3`, then configured `voyage-code-4`. Re-embedded **0** chunks, stored only `voyage-code-3` vectors, and returned identical search scores (0.527 / 0.447) to the no-drift control. Repeated under `CHUNKHOUND_MCP_MODE=1` with stdout confirmed clean.
- `tests/test_smoke.py` plus the provider, matryoshka, drift and config suites: 352 passed.
- 17 new drift tests, covering the pin, the config write-back, an interrupted half-switch, an unreadable database, and provider changes.
- `mypy` clean on all changed modules. No new `ruff` findings.

## Not included

`voyage-context-4` uses a different endpoint (`/v1/contextualizedembeddings`) taking `inputs: List[List[str]]` grouped per document, and depends on per-file grouping that `EmbeddingService._create_token_aware_batches()` does not preserve. Splitting one file's chunks across requests would degrade results silently. It needs a provider-interface change and its own benchmark.

## Breaking changes

None. The default is unchanged, and the new entries are additive.

Two behavior changes worth noting:

- Pointing `embedding.model` at a different model than the index holds no longer re-embeds automatically. Accept the prompt, or delete the database directory and re-index, to adopt a new model.
- An unsupported `output_dims` on a 4-series model now raises at construction instead of at the first API call.

author: zir0-93
body:
## Why

Comparing **two revisions of a 452-file repository** — ~12,000 components each — exhausted a memory budget several times the configured heap and the process was killed by the OS, with **no `OutOfMemoryError`**: most of the excess was native memory outside every `jvm_memory_*` pool. It died **nine seconds into `"Merging old and new code models.."`**, during neither parse.

The merge loop was the obvious suspect and **it was not the cost.** Measuring the constructor phase by phase on a fixed pair of 11,750-component models:

| phase | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `head.copy()` | 23.1 MiB | 24.1 |
| `new ChangeSet` | 392.9 MiB | 94.6 |
| `ExtractedRelationships(merged)` | 182.7 MiB | 44.7 |
| the merge loop itself | 28.3 MiB | 2.5 |
| **total** | **629.2 MiB** | **165.6 (−73.7%)** |

`ChangeSet` and relationship extraction were the cost, because the model's component accessor deep-copies on every read and both resolve every reference in the model through it — extraction three times over per analysis, walking a parent chain per member, taking a copy at each step to read one field.

`head.copy()` rising ~1MiB is clarpse's shared string pool paying for its own map entries, against 227MiB saved beside it.

## A real bug, found by pinning behaviour before changing it

The merge intends to union both revisions' children onto the merged component, so a member deleted by a change still appears inside its surviving parent. It did not: the copying accessor returned a **deep copy**, so `insertChildComponent` mutated a throwaway that was never written back.

The consequence is larger than the dead work. `PUMLClassFieldsCode.generateChangeSummary` counts deleted children by walking `cmp.children()`, so **the deleted-member count in a class header was structurally incapable of being anything but zero.** Deleted methods have never reached a rendered diagram.

**This changes diff output.** It is a behavioural fix, not an optimisation, and it is called out here because a reviewer should expect rendered output to differ. `CodeDiffMergedChildrenTest` pins the intended behaviour and fails on the previous build; an end-to-end test renders a real diff and asserts the deleted method appears. No existing test covered it in either direction.

## Breaking: clarpse 11.0.0's accessor rename, so striff-lib 4.0.0

The two non-copying accessors this PR was built on first landed in clarpse under `live*` names that only made sense next to the ones they were added beside. clarpse 11.0.0 replaces the whole scheme with one rule — **a plain name returns the model's own instance, a `copyOf` prefix returns an isolated deep copy** — and this PR adopts it.

| before | clarpse 11.0.0 | returns |
|---|---|---|
| `getComponent` | `copyOfComponent` | a deep copy |
| `parentBaseCmp` | `copyOfParentBaseComponent` | a deep copy |
| `liveComponent` | `component` | the model's own instance |
| `liveParentBaseCmp` | `parentBaseComponent` | the model's own instance |

Behaviour is identical at all four; only the names moved. 55 call sites here, plus the javadoc and one architecture note that name the old accessors in prose.

The one trap in the sweep: **the old `parentBaseCmp` was the copying variant**, so it maps to `copyOfParentBaseComponent` and *not* to the near-identically named `parentBaseComponent`, which is now the live one. Renaming it by shape rather than by contract would have converted a defensive copy into a live handle on the parsed model with nothing visible in the diff to say so.

**striff-lib goes to 4.0.0.** It hands `OOPSourceCodeModel` to its own callers, so the rename reaches them too — a consumer resolving components through any of the four old names has to move. The mapping is one-to-one and behaviour-preserving.

## The rename exposed a question the sweep does not answer

Most callers of what is now `copyOfComponent` never needed a copy: they read one field off a component and drop it, having paid for a duplicate of its imports, its children and every one of its references. Converting them is where the remaining allocation win is, and converting one wrongly is a **wrong answer rather than a slow one** — a caller that mutates what it is handed would silently start mutating the model. So this is deliberately partial: only sites where the read is obvious from the few lines around it, and where the call is per-component or per-member so the cost scales with the model rather than with the change.

**Converted:**

- `DiagramComponent`'s child filter was a presence test spelled as a deep copy followed by `isPresent()`. It now asks `containsComponent`, which allocates nothing at all, and it runs once per child of every component a diagram is built from.
- `StriffDiagramModel`'s component selection reads a source-file path in one place and a component type in another, and the parent walk beside it reads a name off its result. Nothing survives the iteration.
- `SyntheticModuleAugmenter` walks every changed component for its module name, then every reference of each for the module of its target, keeping neither.
- `SyntheticModuleSupport` reads a source file and a package off each of a module's children. The package case is **provably identical** rather than merely safe: `Package` is immutable and a copied component shares its owner's instance of it, so the copy was already handing back the same object.

**Deliberately left on the copy:**

- Both constructions of a `DiagramComponent` from a model. A `DiagramComponent` retains the component for its whole life and exposes `setName` over it, so the live instance would give every caller of that setter the power to rename a component in the parsed model. Documented at both sites rather than left to be rediscovered by whoever next reads the accessor name and assumes the copy is vestigial.

Every remaining `copyOfComponent` call is in tests, where the allocation does not matter and the isolation is occasionally the point.

## Structural sharing was attempted and is refused

Reusing base's components for files a change does not touch would take two models from ~2x memory to ~1x plus a delta. The hazards were tested rather than assumed, and **rename, package-move, deletion, wildcard imports, nested types and inherited methods all produce identical reference targets across revisions** — simple names resolve speculatively from the file's own text. Sharing looked sound.

The blocker is the **internal/external classification**. A file naming `Widget` with no import resolves it to `com.sample.Widget` at both revisions, but the reference is *external* where no file declares that type and *internal* where one does, and the package graph is built only from internal edges. So the reuse case that looks safest is the one that breaks: **a change that adds a class which unchanged files already referenced** would carry base's `external` classification into head, and a genuinely added dependency would go unreported — a silent false negative, not an error.

Re-classifying every reused component's references would fix it and defeat the purpose. Refused, with `CrossFileResolutionHazardTest` recording the hazard so a future attempt has to pass it.

## Methodology

Allocation is `ThreadMXBean.getThreadAllocatedBytes`, median of three iterations after one warm-up, spread under 0.3% — preferred to wall clock and to `Runtime.freeMemory()` because it is exact and does not depend on when a collection ran. Models are synthetic and deterministic, so two runs build byte-identical inputs and figures are comparable across builds; a parse would dominate both the clock and the allocation figure and add parser variance.

The allocation table above was measured before the rename. The rename moves no behaviour, so the figures stand; the conversions in the section above are additional and unmeasured, and are argued from call frequency rather than from a benchmark.

## Depends on clarpse 11.0.0

`component`, `parentBaseComponent`, `copyOfComponent` and `copyOfParentBaseCom

body:
The **Fault Tolerance and Organizational Resilience Framework** is now filed in the private repository as **addendum 19** (owner decision, 2026-08-18). This repository names it the way `GOVERNANCE.md` established for the constitution and addenda 5, 11 and 15: **by number, without a link**, so the governance structure stays visible where its contents are not.

Docs only.

---

## Why private

It is organizational in kind — duty of care, who is responsible for noticing whom, how a detected failure acquires an owner — which is precisely the material `PUBLIC_PRIVATE_BOUNDARY.md` keeps out of a public repository. Same class as addenda 11 and 15, filed alongside them in `organization/`.

The document is stored verbatim there, byte-identical to the supplied source, under the provenance header this project uses.

## What stays public

Everything technical. `SPEC_RECONCILIATION.md` §28 already carries the §18 disposition (**ACCEPT WITH MODIFICATIONS**), the six modifications, what was built, and the defect the implementation found — because the consequences of a private document are public even where the document is not.

This PR only stops §28 from saying the document is unfiled, and adds the entry to the addenda index:

| | |
|---|---|
| `docs/GOVERNANCE.md` | now names addenda 5, 11, 15 **and 19** as the privately-held set |
| `docs/README.md` | 19 listed in its own group — a later document in the organizational lineage — held privately, pointing at §28 for the disposition |
| `docs/SPEC_RECONCILIATION.md` §28 | says where it lives and why, instead of "not yet filed" |

Every relative link in the root README and all of `docs/` still resolves; the private four remain named-not-linked by design.

author: sfph
body:
## Summary

Clarifies **what PSK actually protects** in Mycelium’s hub-and-spoke model, fixes misleading hub-and-spoke docs, and makes the hub SLIM master secret **durable across `config apply`** by moving it into `config.toml`.

**Core insight:** Mycelium has **two enforcement planes**. Spokes participate over **HTTP (`:8000`)**; the **SLIM/MLS fabric (`:46357`)** is hub-side (moderator + native clients). PSK gates **native SLIM group join** on the hub — it does **not** secure spokes. Shared-hub security is **`auth.enabled` (JWT)**, not a private master secret.

## Background (analysis)

### Two planes

| Plane | Port | Who uses it | Default protection |
|-------|------|-------------|-------------------|
| **HTTP API** | 8000 | Spokes, `memory`, `await`/`respond` | Open (opt-in JWT) |
| **SLIM / MLS** | 46357 | Hub backend moderator; dev `slim send` | PSK on hub |

Spokes are **thin HTTP clients**. The hub holds server-side presence (lease + durable transcript); agents never join MLS on the spoke in the default path.

### What PSK protects (and does not)

- **Does:** authenticates **native SLIM apps** joining a room’s MLS group (`MYCELIUM_SLIM_MASTER_SECRET` → HMAC per `workspace/room` → `create_app_with_secret`).
- **Does not:** HTTP memory/participation, `@handle` impersonation, spoke access, or privacy from the hub operator (backend reads plaintext for transcript/aligner/memory).
- **MLS** encrypts on the fabric; PSK is the room **gate**, not the message cipher.

### Why spokes work without the master secret

`await`/`respond` hit the hub API. PSK is irrelevant to that path — which is why setting a private PSK alone does **not** secure a shared LAN; **`auth.enabled`** does.

### Prior doc problems fixed

- Hub-and-spoke implied spokes “coordinate over SLIM” and need `:46357` + PSK sync.
- Troubleshooting pointed spokes at the SLIM node instead of `:8000`.
- Manual `.env` edits for PSK were unsafe: **`config apply` regenerates `.env` from `config.toml`** and only preserved `MYCELIUM_IMAGE_TAG`.

## Changes in this PR

### Docs
- New **[Security Planes](mycelium-cli/src/mycelium/docs/guides/security-planes.md)** guide (two-plane model, deployment profiles, PSK scope).
- Rewritten **[Hub & Spoke](mycelium-cli/src/mycelium/docs/guides/hub-and-spoke.md)**: spokes → `server.api_url` `:8000`; SLIM optional; hub-only PSK via config.
- Updates to **architecture**, **troubleshooting**, **auth** (HTTP plane callout).

### Hub SLIM PSK — Option A (`config.toml` source of truth)
- `[slim].master_secret` in `MyceliumConfig`.
- **`ensure_slim_master_secret()`** on `config apply` / install: import from legacy `.env` if present, else generate `secrets.token_hex(32)`.
- Rendered to `MYCELIUM_SLIM_MASTER_SECRET` in `.env` for the backend container.
- **`config apply --migrate-env`** imports existing `.env` secret into config.
- **`config show`** masks SLIM PSK; rotation via `config set slim.master_secret`.
- Public dev literal **unchanged** as runtime fallback for tests / host `uvicorn` without Docker.

### CLI / doctor
- **`mycelium connect`**: notes that default participation uses HTTP, not SLIM.
- **`config set slim.identity signerjwt|spire`**: reminds that HTTP auth is separate.
- **`doctor`**: HTTP JWT gate status from `/health`; hub-only SLIM PSK check from `config.toml`.

## Deliberately out of scope

- Spoke-side SLIM connectors / custodial MLS (#667) — documented as future/alternate paths, not changed here.
- `MYCELIUM_SLIM_REQUIRE_SECRET` compose defaults, TLS to SLIM node, per-room PSK epoch rotation.
- Syncing PSK to spokes (they don’t use it).

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/test_slim_master_secret_config.py tests/test_doctor_checks.py tests/test_docker_env_image_tag_pin.py tests/test_docker_env_auth.py`
- [ ] Fresh install → `config apply` → `config show` shows masked SLIM PSK; `.env` contains `MYCELIUM_SLIM_MASTER_SECRET`
- [ ] Re-run `config apply` → secret unchanged in `config.toml` and `.env`
- [ ] Spoke with remote `server.api_url` → `doctor` warns if HTTP auth off; no SLIM PSK check
- [ ] Hub with dev literal in config → `doctor` warns

author: kompfner
body:
Follow-up work to the recent `GoogleLLMService` default model bump to Gemini 3.6 Flash. 

## Fixed a bug when using Gemini 3.7 Flash

`_maybe_unset_thinking_budget` applies `thinking_level: "minimal"` to any model matching `gemini-3*` and `flash`, as a low-latency default. 3.7 Flash rejects `minimal`.

```
gemini-3.7-flash   {'thinking_level': 'minimal'}  -> 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT
    "Thinking level MINIMAL is not supported for this model."
```

It now gets `low`, the lowest level it accepts. Models we don't recognize (so, future models) still get `minimal`, so a new flash model that doesn't support `minimal` will need an entry here, too.

Nothing else about 3.7 needed changing — streaming, function calling, and thought signatures behave as they do on 3.6.

## Added a warning when using `thinking_budget` with Gemini 3 models

On 2.5, `thinking_budget` was the only thinking control. Gemini 3 takes `thinking_level` instead, and what happens to a `thinking_budget` set on its own varies by model *and* by backend:

| `thinking_budget=0` | Gemini API | Vertex |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gemini-2.5-flash | honored | honored |
| gemini-3.5-flash | honored | honored |
| gemini-3.6-flash | **400** | honored |
| gemini-3.7-flash | **ignored** | **ignored** |

The 400 reads `"Request contains an invalid argument."` — it names no field — and the ignored cases produce no signal at all.

The service now emits a warning when a `thinking_budget` is set on a Gemini 3 model, which covers all cases, teaching developers not to use `thinking_budget` with newer Gemini models.

Note: we deliberately chose a warning and not a translation: only `0` and `-1` have honest `thinking_level` equivalents.

## Made `GoogleVertexLLMService` default to `gemini-3.6-flash`

Now it matches `GoogleLLMService`'s default instead of trailing it (it was previously 2.5 flash).

Note that we also had to update the default `location` to "global", which is the location where the Gemini 3 models are available. **This is a behavior change.**

| | us-east4 | us-central1 | global |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gemini-2.5-flash | OK | OK | OK |
| gemini-3.x (all) | 404 | 404 | OK |

3.6 costs some latency on Vertex but stays well inside a voice budget — 0.699s median time to first byte against 0.393s for 2.5-flash, measured through the pipeline over 12 turns, worst case 1.101s.

## Why the default is still 3.6, not the newer 3.7

3.7 is slower at its floor in every configuration measured, because removing `minimal` means its lowest setting still thinks adaptively. Median / p90 time to first token, live API, voice-shaped context:

| scenario | 3.6 @ minimal | 3.7 @ low | 3.7 @ medium (its default) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 16 turns, no tools (n=10) | **0.77 / 0.90** | 0.87 / 1.19 | 1.86 / 2.45 |
| 16 turns, **+ tools** (n=25) | **0.80 / 1.28** | 1.35 / 2.67 | 1.27 / 4.39 |
| 40 turns, no tools (n=20) | **0.79 / 1.06** | 0.90 / 1.71 | 1.85 / 3.13 |
| Vertex global, + tools (n=12) | **0.90 / 2.51** | 1.51 / 2.55 | 2.69 / 3.49 |

With tools attached — the normal state of a voice agent — 3.7 at its floor costs ~550 ms median and ~1.4 s at p90. Pricing is identical, and Google positions 3.7 for "coding and agents" with no latency claims, while 3.6 is the speed-balanced model. 3.6 carries no deprecation notice.

## Testing

New `tests/test_google_thinking_defaults.py` covers the per-model thinking default, the unrecognized-model fallback, the warning, and the Vertex defaults — there was no coverage of this path before, which is how 3.7 shipped broken.

Behavioral evals, all passing:

- Vertex on the new defaults: `weather_function_call`, `multi_turn`
- `gemini-3.7-flash`: `async_tool_delivery`, `async_tool_cancellation`, `async_tool_cancellation_concurrent`, `function_call_timeout`, `weather_function_call`, `weather_and_restaurant`

The async ones matter most: unreliable async-tool reporting is what moved the default off 2.5 in the first place, and 3.7 handles it, including concurrent cancellation.

author: ipjohnson
body:
A first-adopter run against 0.8.0-rc1000 — build a real application from the published packages, follow the public docs, read the source only when something breaks — produced eleven findings. Three were code defects. This closes all three and writes down the plan for the rest.

## The defects

All three were silent, and every one of them was covered by an existing test that could not fail.

**RazorBlade views over ~1 KiB returned HTTP 200 with an empty body.** `HardenedHtmlTemplate.WriteOutput` wrapped a `StreamWriter` around the response body, and RazorBlade's `WriteLiteral` is a synchronous `TextWriter.Write` — so once a view passed the writer's default 1 KiB buffer it flushed synchronously and Kestrel refused, mid-render, after the status line had gone out. Views under 1 KiB were fine, which is why it survived: it is a function of how much a page emits rather than of anything the application does.

Rendering now goes into a pooled buffer and out in one asynchronous write, which is what ASP.NET Core MVC does for the same reason. The tests missed it because they render into a `MemoryStream`, which accepts synchronous writes; `SynchronousWritesRejectedStream` is the double that does not.

**A handler reported the path it was declared with rather than the one it answers.** A handler class is generated from its own declarations, so it knew its controller's `[BasePath]` and not the module's — a route served at `/catalog/books` described itself as `/books`. `IGlobalFilterRegistry`'s per-handler overload is documented as deciding by path, so the documented `handlerInfo.Path.StartsWith("/catalog")` matched nothing and the filter silently never ran, for every route in every library that owns a URL space.

The routing table now passes the path it routed at, composed by the same `RoutePath.Combine` that built the tree — so there is no second implementation of the base-path rules to drift from the first.

**A view could not reach a library module's routes.** Links are generated per module, so an application whose routes live in libraries had an empty `ApplicationLinks`, and that is the type a generated template base hard-types its `Links` property to. `ApplicationLinks` now carries a property per imported module that publishes links, named for the module, so `@Links.CatalogLibrary.Book.ById(id)` binds. Resolved against the compilation rather than assumed, because most modules have no routes and so no links type to name.

## Verification

Each fix has a regression test confirmed to fail against the old code first — 3 of 5 for the template fix, 2 of 3 for the handler path.

Full suite: **4,239 passing, 0 failing.** One public API addition (`ExecutionRequestHandlerInfo.WithPath`); the surface guard caught it and the approved file is updated with that one line.

Verified end to end against a local pack: the audit sample now runs with zero workarounds — the hand-written template base deleted, the audit filter back on the documented `Path.StartsWith` shape, 14 tests green, no server errors.

## Plans

`docs/DOCS-PLAN.md` — nine of the eleven findings were documentation, in four classes that all follow from one structural fact: the docs live in a different repository from the code, so snippets cannot be compiled, inventories cannot be generated, and a package can ship with no page and nothing notices. The guide pages themselves are the asset; the plan does not touch them.

`docs/TEMPLATE-PLAN.md` — templates named for workload, host as an option, and a CI assertion that generating the same project per host differs only in the host project. That turns the framework's central claim into something checked rather than asserted.

Also worth knowing, found while packing locally: the conditional `ProjectReference` in `Hardened.Requests.Runtime.csproj` picks up a sibling `ValidationModules` checkout if one exists, and packs a dependency on a version that was never published. Harmless on a clean machine, silent when it happens.

author: kravisha
body:
Stacked on #14 — base is `docs/addendum-19-reference`. Review after it, or merge #14 first and this retargets to `master` on its own.

---

The lifecycle catalogue has carried an `injectable` flag since it was written — *"whether a scenario can cause this on demand in a live run"* — and for **thirty-six events the answer was yes in the catalogue and no in fact**. Nothing could cause anything.

The fault-tolerance work (#13) made that worse rather than better: it declared four executive-failure events injectable, so the machinery that notices a dead COO had no way to be exercised by the machinery meant to prove it works. The framework's §15 is explicit that the purpose is *"not merely to prove that processes restart"* but to prove the organization notices, assigns responsibility, recovers and learns.

## 1. Three actions, because three are real

The same entry rule the catalogue keeps: a scenario naming a fault nothing can produce would pass by never running.

| | |
|---|---|
| **kill** | `taskkill /F`, not a signal the process could handle. A clean exit is the one thing a crash fault must not cause — the same reasoning `harness.py` already records about uvicorn and `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT`. |
| **stop** | Retirement through the ordinary path. The **control case**: a suite that only ever kills cannot show that a watcher tells a decision apart from a failure, which is the two-axis lifecycle's whole purpose. |
| **lock_database** | An exclusive write lock. §15's "database temporarily unavailable", and the closest thing this architecture has to a network partition, since SQLite is the only coordination channel. |

Named as absent rather than left to be assumed: **hanging** a process needs a suspend primitive Windows does not offer without a debugger or a third dependency; **network partition** has no network to partition; **simultaneous multi-failure** is composition, which a schedule already expresses.

Targets are named by identity and resolved through `agent_registry`, so a fault that cannot find its target says so rather than killing something else. Schedules are parsed at scenario **load**, because a fault that turns out to be unspellable at second 40 of a five-minute run has wasted the run.

## 2. Two defects the first fault scenario found

**The harness could not run any scenario that changed the population.** Readiness was computed from the harness process's own `BASELINE_POPULATION` defaults, so a scenario staffing judgment at zero waited the full 60s for agents nobody had asked for, then failed a run that had started correctly. Every scenario until now used the default, so the harness had never been asked the question.

**A property that passed without measuring anything.** `population.respawns` counts completed spawn *directives*, and a COO recovery deliberately bypasses the queue — so it read `0` through a run that had killed and replaced an executive. A property that passes whether or not the feature ran is worse than no property. The assertion moved to `incidents.total`, where a watch that kept respawning would file a second incident and a third.

## 3. Verification

**1257 passed** (was 1246).

`executive_failure` run against a live organization — a real backend, real agent processes, a real kill:

```
[harness] fault kill coo-1 at +20s: killed coo-1 (pid 35116)
ready in   2.5s
shutdown   clean - teardown ran and no agent is left running

properties: 6/6 passed
  [PASS] the failure was noticed at all: 1 >= 1
  [PASS] the organization recovered without being told: 1 >= 1
  [PASS] nobody had to be escalated to: 0 == 0
  [PASS] the failure was detected once, not in a loop: 1 == 1
  [PASS] the workforce was not disturbed by the executive's failure: 0 == 0
  [PASS] no agent ended the run believing it had crashed: len([]) == 0
```

The `incidents.*` metric family added in #13 exists for exactly this: without it a fault scenario could observe that a process restarted, but not that the organization *noticed*.

## 4. What this does not do

It does not implement §15's remaining scenarios — manager killed while subordinates live, worker disappears holding work, repeated crash/restart loop, recovery process itself failing. The mechanism is here and each is now a YAML file; they land one at a time, with a run behind each, rather than thirteen at once.

author: ashleeradka
body:
## TL;DR

Follow-up to #40882, which fixed the inverted envelopes on notifications. Conversations expressed the same read/unread state with a **different icon family** (`CircleCheck` / `Circle`) that named the command rather than the state. One module now owns read-state iconography for the whole client, and every read/unread control reads from it. The group menu's copy moves into the chat catalog in the same pass, since it was the last hardcoded menu sitting beside a converted one.

Part of LUM-3336

## Before / after

| Surface | Control | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conversation menu (sidebar, header, mobile sheet) | "Mark as read" (conversation is unread) | Filled check circle | Sealed envelope |
| Conversation menu | "Mark as unread" (conversation is read) | Empty circle | Opened envelope |
| Sidebar section menu | "Mark All as Read" | Filled check circle | Check-marked envelope |
| Sidebar section menu | Every label, plus the mobile sheet title | Hardcoded English | Same English, from the catalog |
| Notifications (feed, detail panels, bell) | Read/unread toggle | Envelope pair (fixed in #40882) | unchanged |

No behaviour, wiring, or English copy changes. Only glyphs and where the strings come from.

## The rule, in one place

`clients/web/src/utils/read-state-icon.ts` states it and exports it:

- A per-item read/unread glyph names **the state the item is in**, never the command: sealed for unread, opened for read. That is what keeps it agreeing with the unread dot on the same row, which is the confusion the original report hit.
- The control's **label** names the command ("Mark as read").
- A **bulk** command names no single item's state, and reusing a state glyph for it would put two envelopes with opposite meanings a row apart in the same sidebar. It takes the check-marked envelope (`MailCheck`), which reads as a command in the same family.

`buildReadToggle` in the home domain reads from the same module, so notifications and conversations cannot drift apart again. It lives in `utils/` beside `channel-presentation.tsx`, the existing top-level icon-mapping module, because chat and home cannot import each other (`local/no-cross-domain-imports`).

## Group menu copy

`group-actions-menu.tsx` held ten hardcoded labels and a concatenated sheet title (`{label} actions`) while `conversation-actions-menu.tsx` next to it already went through `t()`. Both renderers now take a namespace-bound `t` (the pattern the conversation menu uses), `GroupActionsMenu` and `ConversationNavSection` supply it, the strings live in `chat.json` for `en` and `es`, and the file is added to `i18nEnforcedPaths` so `local/no-untranslated-strings` holds the line.

## Why it is safe

- Presentation and copy plumbing only: no state shape, predicate, or mutation changed. Which read/unread branch renders is still decided by `onMarkRead` vs `onMarkUnread`, wired from `hasUnseenLatestAssistantMessage` (header) and `canMarkRead` (row), both verified to mean "unread" on the mark-read branch.
- English copy is byte-identical to what was hardcoded, so the existing group-menu tests assert the same strings through the catalog.
- Verified live in Storybook: an unread conversation's menu renders `lucide-mail` on "Mark as read", a read one renders `lucide-mail-open` on "Mark as unread", and the section menu renders `lucide-mail-check` on "Mark All as Read" with every label resolving through the catalog.
- New tests in `conversation-actions-menu.test.tsx` pin both per-item cases (the unread case also rules out the open glyph explicitly, since `lucide-mail` is a prefix of `lucide-mail-open`). `read-toggle.test.ts` still pins the notification side.
- Typecheck and lint clean, including the newly enforced i18n path. Suites run in CI.

## Swept for the same class of mistake

Every state-conditional icon in the client was reviewed. The rest name commands next to a text label with no adjacent state indicator to contradict (`isPinned ? PinOff : Pin` across five call sites, archive/unarchive, fullscreen, play/stop), or already name state (`isDirectory ? Folder : FileText`, `isInbound ? Inbox : Send`). Read/unread was the only pair naming the command while sitting beside a state dot, and it is now the only pair with a shared definition.

author: eadanp
body:
Adds a client for the [ANI Planner API](https://docs.outboundiq.cloud/reference/ani-planner/), which analyzes recent dial volume against current ANI inventory and recommends how many numbers to provision per region.

## Usage

```ts
const plan = await oiq.aniPlanner.generate({
  dateStart: "2026-05-01",
  dateEnd: "2026-05-28",
  dailyDialsTarget: "BETTER",   // 50 | 75 | 100 dials per ANI per day
  groupBy: "area_code",          // "area_code" | "ani" | "zip"
  inventoryMode: "managed",      // "managed" | "all"
  campaigns: ["west-coast-outbound"],
});

if (plan.success) {
  for (const r of plan.data.regionStats) {
    if (r.difference > 0) console.log(`${r.region}, ${r.state}: add ${r.difference}`);
  }
}
```

Every request field is optional, so `generate()` with no arguments analyzes the start of the current month through yesterday across every campaign.

## Changes

- `src/resources/aniPlanner.ts` — `AniPlannerResource.generate()` wrapping `POST /ani-planner/generate`, plus `AniPlannerGenerateRequest`, `AniPlannerGenerateResponse`, `AniPlannerPlan`, `AniPlannerRegionStat`, `AniPlannerCampaign`, and the `AniPlannerDailyDialsTarget` / `AniPlannerGroupBy` / `AniPlannerInventoryMode` / `AniPlannerCountry` unions.
- Registered as `oiq.aniPlanner` and re-exported from the package entry point.
- README section and feature-list mention.
- Minor changeset.

## Notes on the shape

- The response is a discriminated union (`{ success: true; data }` / `{ success: false; message }`), mirroring `AssignmentResponse`. Documented failures (400/401/403) still surface as thrown `APIError` / `AuthenticationError` from the HTTP layer.
- `country` is widened with `(string & {})` and `AniPlannerPlan` keeps an index signature, matching the forward-compat approach already used in `dials.ts` and `nrm.ts`.
- JSDoc carries the semantics the docs spell out: the 20 dials/business-day threshold, why `aniDifference` reflects surplus held in low-volume regions, when `missingZipData` fires, and how `regionStats` differs by country.

## Verification

`npm run typecheck` clean, 46 tests pass (2 new — endpoint/body/response shape and the empty-body default), `npm run build` succeeds.

author: beesmf96
body:
Plan: `.claude/plans/plan-change-password.md`

## The problem

There is no authenticated change-password feature. `UpdateUserRequest` allows only `name`, `phone`, and `preferred_location`, and the reset routes sit inside `Route::middleware('guest')` — so a logged-in user is redirected away from them. The only path to a new password was logging out and using the emailed reset link.

Google accounts were worse off. `GoogleAuthController` created them with `Str::random(32)`, hashed by `User::casts()`. That is a real password hash of a value nobody knows — indistinguishable in the database from a password the user chose, and impossible to confirm on a change-password form.

## The approach

New OAuth accounts are created with `password => null`. That null is the only signal that an account has no password the user could type, and `UpdatePasswordRequest` drops the `current_password` requirement for exactly those accounts.

**Detecting OAuth accounts by `google_id` would be wrong**, which is worth stating because it is the obvious shortcut: a user who registered with a password and later signed in with Google has *both* — `GoogleAuthController` links them — and must still confirm their current password. The check is `password === null`, never `google_id !== null`.

Product decision behind this: a Google user may set a password and afterwards sign in either way. That matches the linking behaviour the controller already had in the reverse direction.

## What's here

- `PUT /profile/password` → `Auth\PasswordController@update`, in the existing `verified` group, `throttle:5,1` like the other auth routes. Named `profile.password.update` — `password.update` already belongs to the reset flow.
- `UpdatePasswordRequest` — `current_password` required unless the user has none; new password `min:8|confirmed`, matching `ResetPasswordController`.
- `Profile.vue` — a second card, reading "Change Password" or "Set a Password" depending on the new `hasPassword` prop.
- `GoogleAuthController` — `password => null`, and the now-unused `Str` import removed.

Two subtleties worth a reviewer's eye:

- **`password` is outside `$fillable`**, so `update()` silently drops it. This uses `forceFill([...])->save()`, as `ResetPasswordController` does.
- **No login guard was needed.** Laravel's `BcryptHasher::check()` returns false for a null hash, so a passwordless account cannot be logged into by password. There's a test asserting this rather than trusting it.

## Known limitation

Existing OAuth rows keep their random hash and will see the "change" form they cannot satisfy. A blanket `UPDATE users SET password = NULL WHERE google_id IS NOT NULL` would destroy the real password of anyone who linked Google to a password account — indistinguishable in the current schema. Affected users can use forgot-password. Only a few such accounts exist, all on dev.

## Docs

`.claude/CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/agents/coder.md` both documented the random-hash behaviour. Updated, along with a note that `password` needs `forceFill`.

## Verification

- `php artisan test` — **373 passed**, 1297 assertions
- `bun run test --run` — **107 passed** (14 files)
- Line coverage **98.50%** (1186/1204), above the `MIN_COVERAGE: 95` gate; `PasswordController` and `UpdatePasswordRequest` both 100%
- `vendor/bin/pint` clean; `bun run lint` 0 errors, warning count unchanged from the base branch

`tests/Feature/Auth/GoogleAuthTest` had an assertion pinning the old random-hash behaviour; it now asserts null, with a comment explaining why.

author: dipotheone-lang
body:
Step 1 of the execution order of 18-Aug-2026 — "load answers into config" — plus the intake analysis of the order itself.

## What the step actually buys

The order projects that **ten of twelve** class 1 obligations activate immediately. **Four** do: `STAT-VAT`, `STAT-WHT`, `STAT-SOCINS`, `STAT-CIT`. The other eight have no computable date, and the report now says so as a share rather than as eight technical lines.

## The defect that mattered

`"7 days from rejection"` — the ETA clearance window, whose clock starts when ETA rejects an invoice — matched the day-of-month branch on its leading `7` and became **day 7 of the month**. An event-driven statutory window had silently become a fixed monthly date. §2.1 rates a confidently wrong date worse than no date at all, and this is the tightest window in the system.

Event windows are now refused before every other branch, because each later branch finds a number in them and turns it into a calendar date.

## Code changes

**`parse_due`** learns the shapes the order uses: event windows (refused, with the reason), month-end, month-end with a working-day lead, annual dates by name. `_apply_lead` subtracts working days on a Sunday–Thursday week, so the operative date moves earlier without the statutory anchor moving.

**`build_statutory`** states coverage as a share — *"4 of 12 class 1 obligations have a usable date"* — and counts the two kinds of silence apart: six await a date, two are event-driven and await the event register. Both are silence; the remedies differ, and a merged count would send the CEO to the wrong person.

The provenance line now distinguishes three states that shared one message: tracking nothing, tracking CEO-stated dates, tracking dates with no recorded provenance at all. `ceo_stated` is not `verified_by_advisor` and never becomes it by time passing — §7 of the order makes promotion without a named human a stop condition.

**`_horizon_section`** carries its caveat whether or not the horizon is populated. It fired only on an empty horizon, which had it backwards: a horizon showing four dates is the one a reader mistakes for coverage.

**`config/statutory-calendar.yaml`** carries the twelve rules with `provenance: ceo_stated` on every row, and `owner` / `preparer` / `escalation` throughout. `STAT-LIC` and the ownership fields were lost in an earlier rewrite of this file and recovered by the tests that assert §2.1's list is complete.

## `docs/decisions/EXECUTION-ORDER-CONFLICTS.md`

The order says it wins on conflict, and Control operates on that. §17 says Control may never edit the charter, so the disagreements are recorded for the CEO rather than reconciled. **Five need a decision:**

1. **Four D-numbers carry two decisions each.** Appendix B runs to D-14; the order runs to D-53 and says Appendix B extends to it. D-10, D-11, D-13 and D-14 collide. No substantive disagreement — each pair is two unrelated decisions sharing a number, and all eight are in force. But charter D-14 is the authority under which Stage C OCRs scanned client-confidential contracts, and §12.1.2 lists OCR under *prohibited, absolutely*. Overwriting that number turns a shipped exception into a breach.
2. **Charter version.** The order cites v4.2 + §18; the repository is on v4.10, dated the day before. Probably shorthand — if literal, ten decisions and fifteen resolved findings are withdrawn.
3. **§18 does not exist.** B8, B9 and B10 depend on it. Their intent is legible from one-line summaries, but building from a summary is inventing a rule (§1.3).
4. **M2, M4 and M5 are undefined.** D-52's acceptance of legal risk is conditional on M1–M5; only M1 and M3 appear anywhere.
5. **D-52 versus §12.** §12 says Phase 2 does not begin until every item is closed, with counsel; the order says it proceeds on CEO-stated positions with no counsel engaged. Control follows the order — but §5.6 halts on a state the charter does not permit, and §12 is never-learnable, so only the CEO can reconcile them.

Also recorded, no action needed unless the reading is wrong: D-32 implemented as a property of the register rather than a thirteenth row; three charter decisions the order does not mention staying live (D-06's review falls due 16-Sep-2026); the unsigned authorisation block; and that §2.4/§2.5 answer most of the counsel pack, which should now go out as *confirm-or-correct* rather than *please-supply*.

## Tests

660 passing. Seven encoded the superseded "nothing is known yet" invariant and are **updated rather than deleted** — each docstring says what it used to guard and why that survives:

| Test | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `test_partial_statutory_coverage_never_reads_as_coverage` | tracked nothing | four track; the dark share is still the loudest line |
| `test_the_rejection_window_carries_a_number_only_with_its_source` | window is null | window is 7, and must name its source |
| `test_no_statutory_rule_claims_more_than_the_CEO_said` | every rule UNVERIFIED | every rule `ceo_stated`, none advisor-verified |
| `test_a_partial_register_reads_as_partial_not_as_clear` | empty register | partial register, stated as a share |

author: dkneeland
body:
## Phase 0 — Tesla BLE crypto/protobuf de-risk (bench-only)

De-risks the hard parts of the Tesla vehicle-command integration (`ADR 0001`)
without touching any BLE wiring: vendor the Apache-2.0 protos + nanopb runtime,
and implement + prove the mbedTLS 3.6 crypto and session layers against Tesla's
own published test vectors.

> Note on this PR's base: `dkneeland/main` is behind `softwiredtech/dashkit-firmware`
> main by a few commits (it's an older fork mirror). The `feat/tesla-ble-phase0`
> branch itself is based on current upstream main, so the diff here necessarily
> includes those upstream commits that aren't in the fork yet. It cleans right
> up when this is finally opened against the primary repo.

## What's included (commit per concern)

- **Vendor protos + nanopb runtime** (`components/tesla-protocol/`):
  `.proto` files from `teslamotors/vehicle-command` pinned in `protos/VERSION`
  at `f97fa1e4…`, nanopb 0.4.9.1 runtime (7 files, BSD-3-Clause). Not linked
  into firmware yet — they compile and wait for Phase 2 bindings.
- **Crypto layer** (`crypto.c`): P-256 ECDH → `K = SHA1(X)[:16]`, SHA-1 /
  SHA-256 / HMAC-SHA256 (`SESSION_INFO_KEY`, `AUTH_CMD_KEY`), AES-128-GCM
  (`AAD = SHA256(metadata)`), on-curve public-key validation — all on the
  mbedTLS 3.6 API shipped by ESP-IDF 5.4.1.
- **Session layer** (`session.c`): metadata TLV sort/build, session-info HMAC
  auth, request-hash with VCSEC 17-byte truncation.
- **Known-answer tests** (`tools/test/test_tesla_crypto.c` + runner).
- **CI**: host `test` job alongside the firmware `build` job.
- **`.gitattributes`** (`*.sh text eol=lf`) so the host tests run from a
  Windows checkout (also shipped separately as PR #54).

## Verified

- 61/61 known-answer checks vs Tesla's `protocol.md` vectors (ECDH→K both
  directions, `SESSION_INFO_KEY`, session-info HMAC tag, full AES-GCM command
  example, metadata serialization byte-for-byte + independent checksum vector,
  request-hash rules, sign→verify→response-decrypt round trip, tamper/off-curve
  negatives). Host mbedTLS 3.6.2 (same major.minor as the IDF vendored copy).
- Regression-free by construction: clean `main` build and Phase-0 build produce
  byte-identical images except the app-descriptor timestamp (`tesla_*` symbols
  count 0 in the image).
- No protocol code touches BLE yet (Phase 1's scan spike comes next, stacked on
  this branch).

## Not in this phase (deliberately)

nanopb generated bindings, `gen_proto.py`, counter/epoch/clock-offset session
state, all `main/tesla/` code, and any BLE/scan wiring — each has its explicit
phase in the integration plan (`docs/tesla-ble-integration-plan.md`).

author: nakasar
body:
Deuxième étape de l'adoption de Cache Components. La première avait activé le drapeau sans rien changer au rendu ; celle-ci débloque le gain, et c'était plus structurant que prévu.

## Le constat, mesuré

Le layout racine lisait la langue dans un cookie, au sommet de l'arbre. Pour savoir ce que ça coûtait, j'ai retiré l'opt-out de `/about` seule — une page sans la moindre lecture dynamique, du contenu pur.

Elle est ressortie en **`ƒ`**.

Autrement dit : **aucune route de l'application ne pouvait devenir instantanée**, et retirer les 159 autres opt-outs n'y aurait rien changé. Le layout bloquait pour tout le monde.

Ce n'est pas une limite de next-intl mais une propriété inhérente : une coquille statique se préfabrique **par URL**, et une même URL qui rend différemment selon le cookie n'a pas de coquille à préfabriquer. La langue devait entrer dans l'adresse.

## Ce que ça change pour les visiteurs

**Rien.** `localePrefix: "as-needed"` garde le français — la langue par défaut — sans préfixe : `/about` reste `/about`. Seules les autres langues prennent le leur (`/en/about`, `/it/about`, `/de/about`). Aucune adresse existante ne change, donc rien à rediriger ni à réindexer.

## Le résultat

Lu dans la table des routes :

| | coquille statique |
|---|---|
| avant | **0** route — tout en `ƒ` |
| après | **41 `○`** entièrement statiques + **414 `◐`** à coquille partielle |

`/fr/about` et `/en/about` sortent désormais en `○`.

## Ce que ça a demandé

- Les **162 pages** passent sous `app/[locale]/`. Les **185 routes d'API** et les adresses de découverte (`.well-known`, plans de site, `robots.txt`, MCP) restent à la racine : elles ne parlent aucune langue.
- Le **proxy** compose la résolution de langue avec le CORS existant, chacun sur sa famille d'adresses. Aucun en-tête CORS n'est ajouté aux pages — le proxy ne tournait jusqu'ici que sur `/api/`, et ce n'est pas à cette migration d'élargir ça.
- Le **layout racine** déclare ses quatre langues à la construction (`generateStaticParams`) et fixe la locale du sous-arbre (`setRequestLocale`) au lieu de la lire. Son opt-out disparaît.
- **Huit écrans entièrement client** reçoivent une enveloppe serveur. `instant` ne s'exporte pas d'un module `"use client"` (`E1344`), et leur contenu tient entièrement au paramètre d'URL : un `<Suspense>` global n'y aurait produit que la coquille vide contre laquelle [la documentation met explicitement en garde](https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/blocking-prerender-client-hook). Leur décision de rendu est différée sous le TODO prévu pour ça, comme le second motif documenté le prévoit.

## Un test a fait son travail

`ADVERTISED_PATHS` vérifie que chaque adresse annoncée dans le catalogue d'API a bien un fichier derrière elle — il existe précisément pour attraper « renommer une page casse l'annonce en silence ». Les fichiers ayant bougé, il a échoué. Il cherche désormais dans les deux arbres ; **les adresses annoncées, elles, sont inchangées**.

## Ce qui reste, et pourquoi ce n'est pas une régression

Les liens internes utilisent encore `next/link` (168 fichiers) et `next/navigation` (198 fichiers). Le proxy détecte la langue au cookie puis à `accept-language` et redirige vers le préfixe : **un visiteur anglophone reste donc en anglais**, au prix d'un saut de redirection par navigation. Les basculer vers la navigation localisée supprime ce saut — c'est la PR suivante, mécanique et à part.

## Vérification

- `next build --debug-prerender` : **891 pages, aucune route bloquante**, `exit 0`. Le drapeau compte : il désactive l'arrêt à la première erreur, donc la liste vide est bien vide.
- `npm test` : **1008 tests, 0 échec**.
- `node scripts/check-flex-rows.mjs` : sort en succès.
- Build lancé sur **base Mongo semée**, la méthode retenue après l'étape précédente — une base vide laisse passer des erreurs que la production révèle.

**Vérification navigateur : absente.** Le conteneur n'a pas de navigateur et le préaperçu est derrière la protection de déploiement Vercel. C'est la plus grosse réserve de cette PR : le build prouve que les routes prérendent, pas ce qu'elles affichent. À regarder avant de fusionner — l'accueil, une page dans une langue non française (`/en`), et le sélecteur de langue.

author: lifted-truck
body:
**gui2 goes 30/105 → 105/105.** Every declared parameter is now reachable, so every feature is testable.

## The lever was already built and unused

`src/param_presentation.tsv` had 181 rows with an empty `chunk` column, and `gen_gui_controls.py` generates a control for every row whose chunk is named. Naming them — chunk = the row's own group, slugified, so generated markup lands in group-sized clusters rather than one wall — took one pass: **75 controls across 3 pages**, `gui_reach` GREEN.

This is FOUNDATIONS' D1 ruling paying out: structure **derived** from declarations, not hand-placed. The alternative was hand-writing 75 controls — the triple-maintenance scar their standing GUI criterion exists to prevent, and what this would otherwise have cost a day.

## The enum complaint is fixed as a side effect

The generator reads enum labels from the shell, so `select`-declared params now render as **real dropdowns with real option text** (`Off · Drive · Filter · Gain · Comp`) rather than the *"incoherent numeric sliders"* reported on 2026-08-17. Nobody wrote those labels twice — they come from `kParams` and cannot drift.

## Verified in the browser, not inferred from the count

117 controls across four pages (MAIN 29 · MIX 34 · FX 12 · OSC 42), four dropdowns carrying shell labels, **zero JS errors, zero duplicate ids**. Four controls report no `<label>` — the hand-written M/S buttons, whose glyph *is* the label; checked rather than assumed.

## What this does and does not mean

Every parameter is **reachable** and therefore testable. It does **not** mean the layout is designed — 42 controls on OSC in group clusters is a generated surface, not a considered one, and the GUI pass deferred earlier is still owed. Reach first, taste after; that ordering was the point.

author: vikasgaddu1
body:
## Why

The Cost page's existing value map plots **AI curriculum depth** against price. Robotics is scored separately and the two pull apart hard — UIUC sits near the top of the field on AI (4.67) and near the bottom on robotics (3/5, three courses, no credential). A shortlist built around robotics had no view of what the money actually buys on that axis.

## The chart

Scatter of **researched robotics curriculum (1–5) against cost for an NC resident**, with **bubble size carrying robotics access** — labs, teams and undergraduate research you can get into.

A dashed threshold marks the **4/5 curriculum bar** the balanced shortlist already uses before it will auto-pick a school, so the shaded band below it is exactly the group that page declines to recommend.

## The analytical part: the efficient frontier

A school is ringed and named only when **nothing else on the list is both no more expensive and no weaker on robotics.** Three qualify:

| School | Cost | Robotics curriculum |
|---|---|---|
| UNC Chapel Hill | $27,766 | 3/5 |
| NC State | $28,490 | **4/5** |
| Michigan-Dearborn | $50,654 | **5/5** |

Every other school is beaten outright on one axis or the other. That's a far more useful summary than 33 anonymous dots — and it makes NC State's position concrete: at $28,490 with 4/5 robotics, nothing cheaper comes close on robotics coursework.

The callout is explicit that this is **published sticker price only**, so it should be re-read after net-price figures rather than before — aid moves the horizontal axis a long way at the private schools.

## Chart construction

Followed the house dataviz guidance, which caught three things:

- **A 2px surface ring on every marker.** A four-value ordinal y-axis stacks most of the field on two lines; without rings the overlapping dots merge into blobs.
- **Selective labels, not one per point.** Only the frontier schools are named; the axis and hover tooltip carry the rest.
- **A legend, since colour carries meaning** (fit tier), matching the bar chart above it.

Tooltips show cost, curriculum, access, undergraduate robotics course count, and credential type.

## Verification

Rendered the built page in Chromium rather than eyeballing the code — which is how I caught that **Michigan-Dearborn's label was being clipped clean out of the plot area**, since a school at the top of the 1–5 domain has no room above its marker. Labels now flip below at the top of the domain.

`npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build` both pass. Only `Cost.tsx` changes — the throwaway Playwright install used for the screenshot was reverted out.

author: pthirun
body:
## Problem Statement

`SparkChunkAssembler#assembleChunks` caught every exception from `ChunkAssembler#assembleAndGetValue` (except `IllegalStateException`) and returned `null`. The caller (`ChunkAssemblyFunction` in `AbstractDataWriterSparkJob`) treats a `null` result as a legitimate empty/deleted record, so keys with missing/incomplete chunks, byte-count mismatches, or offset-ordering violations were silently dropped instead of failing the task.

`VeniceKafkaInputReducer#extractChunkedMessage` (the MR reducer) calls the same `ChunkAssembler#assembleAndGetValue` with no try/catch, so identical malformed input fails the MR task loudly. This is a correctness gap between the two push-job engines introduced during the MR-to-Spark migration that could cause silent data loss in Spark-based pushes.

`ChunkAssembler#assembleAndGetValue` only returns `null` for two legitimate "no data" outcomes: DELETE with no RMD, or orphan chunks with no manifest ever found. Every exception it throws (missing chunks, byte-count mismatch, offset-ordering violation, unrecognized schema id) represents a genuinely corrupt/incomplete record.

## Solution

- Removed the blanket `catch (Exception e) { return null; }` in `SparkChunkAssembler#assembleChunks`. Exceptions from `ChunkAssembler#assembleAndGetValue` now propagate and fail the Spark task, matching MR's behavior.
- Updated the method's Javadoc and a stale comment in `AbstractDataWriterSparkJob` to reflect that "incomplete chunks" now throws rather than returning `null`.
- `null` is still returned only for the two legitimate no-data cases (DELETE with no RMD, orphan chunks with no manifest); every other failure now surfaces instead of being silently swallowed.

### Code changes

- [ ] Added new code behind **a config**. If so list the config names and their default values in the PR description.
- [ ] Introduced new **log lines**.
  - [ ] Confirmed if logs need to be **rate limited** to avoid excessive logging.

### **Concurrency-Specific Checks**

Both reviewer and PR author to verify

- [x] Code has **no race conditions** or **thread safety issues**.
- [x] Proper **synchronization mechanisms** (e.g., `synchronized`, `RWLock`) are used where needed.
- [x] No **blocking calls** inside critical sections that could lead to deadlocks or performance degradation.
- [x] Verified **thread-safe collections** are used (e.g., `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`).
- [x] Validated proper exception handling in multi-threaded code to avoid silent thread termination.

## How was this PR tested?

- [x] New unit tests added.
- [ ] New integration tests added.
- [x] Modified or extended existing tests.
- [x] Verified backward compatibility (if applicable).

Added a regression test, `testMissingChunksPropagateInSparkSameAsMR`, that feeds identical malformed input (a manifest declaring 2 chunks, but only 1 chunk present) into both paths:
- `SparkChunkAssembler#assembleChunks` now throws `VeniceException` ("Missing 1 / 2 chunks").
- `ChunkAssembler#assembleAndGetValue` called directly (simulating the MR reducer path) throws the same exception.

Ran `./gradlew :clients:venice-push-job:test --tests "com.linkedin.venice.spark.chunk.SparkChunkAssemblerTest"` (all 15 tests pass, including the new regression test) and the full `:clients:venice-push-job:test` module suite (all pass).

## Does this PR introduce any user-facing or breaking changes?

- [ ] No. You can skip the rest of this section.
- [x] Yes. Clearly explain the behavior change and its impact.

Spark-based pushes that hit genuinely corrupt/incomplete chunked records (missing chunks, byte-count mismatch, offset-ordering violation, unrecognized schema id) will now **fail the push job** instead of silently dropping the affected record, matching MapReduce's existing behavior. This is intentional — it closes a silent-data-loss gap — but it means previously-"successful" Spark pushes with such malformed input will now surface as failures.

author: rbuergi
body:
Closes #1866.

`NeverCompiledFailureRedriveTest`'s bounded assertions were anchored on a barrier that a **replayed** emission satisfies, so the assertion pinning the automatic re-drive's **bound** — `ABrokenSource_IsReDrivenExactlyOnce_AndThenLeftAlone`, which is what keeps a permanently-broken NodeType out of an unbounded retry loop on the per-NodeType hub's single-threaded action block — could pass without observing anything.

#1825 added the test; #1850 fixed the *first* race in the same barrier (it waited to *see* a record that is transient by construction). This is the second one it left behind.

## The defect — not a race, an identity

```csharp
var forgedVersion = forged.Version;                       // ← what Update() returned
await workspace.GetMeshNodeStream(typePath)
    .Should().Within(20.Seconds())
    .Match(n => n.Version >= forgedVersion);
```

- `Update` on a foreign path is `UpdateRemote`, which emits **`update(current)`** — the *optimistic local snapshot*; the queue "does NOT wait for the patch's echo from the owner". The forge lambda rewrites `Content` only, so the returned node carries the **pre-write** `Version`.
- `GetMeshNodeStream(path)` is a **`Replay(1)`** mirror (`new ReplaySubject<MeshNode>(1)` per cache entry): a new subscription is handed the snapshot already held.

So `>= forged.Version` is a bound **the stream is already sitting on**. The barrier passes whether or not the write landed, and everything downstream is anchored before the forge. In `ABrokenSource_…` the next `Match` waits for `Error && FailedBuildInputs` — for a type that cannot compile, byte-identical to the record that was already there.

Printed by the barrier itself on the real mesh, twice in one run:

```
the mirror was replaying v6, Update handed back v6 (the SAME revision — so the old '>= 6' bound
was already satisfied), owner then moved to v7.
the mirror was replaying v7, Update handed back v7 (the SAME revision — so the old '>= 7' bound
was already satisfied), owner then moved to v8.
```

And the negative assertion had **no anchor at all**. The window it *means* opens where the caller stands; the window `NotEmit` *observes* opens when its `SubscribeOn(TaskPoolScheduler)` attach lands — and `Replay(1)` collapses everything between into one snapshot. A whole `Pending → Compiling → Error` cycle fits in that gap. Its docstring claimed non-vacuity on the strength of sibling assertions that are different subscriptions and never assert a `Pending`/`Compiling` value reached anyone.

## The fix — a version watermark, plus the ledger as the primary bound

New `RedriveObservation` / `RedriveWindow` (test-side vocabulary, shared by the mesh tests and the proof):

- **Watermark.** The barrier becomes strict (`Version > watermark`) and the anchor is threaded into every observation downstream of the forge. 🚨 **Whose version:** the **owner's**, and a strict *lower bound*, not a receipt — `MeshNode.Version` is minted by the owning hub for **every** writer (`NextVersion` = `current + 1`; #1833 flaked on assuming it tracks the caller's own write). It claims exactly one thing: the owner committed at least one revision past the state this write was diffed against, so no later emission can be that state replayed. Said in those words in the code.
- **Ledger (primary).** `NodeTypeCompileParkRegistry` counts *events* — `RecordFailureRedrive` per automatic kickoff, `RecordAttempt` per real Roslyn dispatch (`RunCompile`). A counter cannot be replayed or conflated and can tell "the re-drive ran and re-failed" apart from "I was handed the pre-forge snapshot back". The window captures both counters where the *caller* stands, not where `NotEmit` happens to attach. The stream observation stays as independent corroboration.

## Non-vacuity — both halves, because "it passes" proves nothing here

`NeverCompiledFailureRedriveTest` is **10/10 green locally on `origin/main`** (class-level, 10 iterations, 75a70c20f). A false green survives its own fix, so the evidence is a **constructed replay**, not a repeat run.

`RedriveObservationReplayTest` (new; a real `ReplaySubject<MeshNode>(1)`, a real `NodeTypeCompileParkRegistry`, no mesh — 4.4 s):

```
Passed  TheOldForgeBarrier_IsSatisfiedByTheReplayedPreForgeSnapshot
  Update returned version 7; the mirror already holds version 7. The old bound is '>= 7'.
  OLD BARRIER ACCEPTED the replay: version 7,
    CompilationError='CS0103: The name 'ThisSymbolDoesNotExist' does not exist',
    FailedBuildInputs='fw=1.0|mods=abc|src=42' — no forge in it.
  NEW BARRIER REJECTED the same replay (watermark v7).
  NEW BARRIER ACCEPTED the genuine owner-minted revision v8.

Passed  TheOldNegativeAssertion_IsSatisfiedByAReplayThatHidesAWholeReDrive
  OLD NEGATIVE ASSERTION PASSED while the ledger recorded re-drive 2 and attempt 2 —
    a FALSE GREEN on the bound that keeps a permanently-broken NodeType out of an unbounded
    retry loop.
  NEW NEGATIVE ASSERTION REJECTED the same replay: Expected value to be 1 … but found 2.

Passed  TheNewNegativeAssertion_AcceptsAQuietWindow          ← the fix is not "assert false"
Passed  TheNewNegativeAssertion_CatchesADriveThatOnlyTheMirrorSaw ← the two witnesses are independent
Passed  TheWatermarkRejectsOnlyTheReplay                     ← the anchor rejects the replay, not newer state
```

## Verification

| | |
|---|---|
| `dotnet build … -c Release -p:CIRun=true -warnaserror` | 0 Warning(s), 0 Error(s) |
| `NeverCompiledFailureRedriveTest`, class-level, BEFORE (origin/main) | **10/10 pass** |
| `NeverCompiledFailureRedriveTest` + `RedriveObservationReplayTest`, class-level, AFTER | ****10/10 pass** (80 test executions)** |

No "What's New" entry: test-only change, no user-visible effect.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

author: ausfarr
body:
Answers "are we using the correct Gemini API for pure image generation": no — Etch was calling models.generateContent, the general-purpose multimodal chat endpoint behind gemini-2.5-flash-image. That model is free to respond with text instead of an image, which is exactly what the reported failure showed: Gemini replied "Here are your whimsical cottagecore mushroom cottages from a bird's-eye view..." instead of drawing anything. No amount of retrying or better diagnostics fixes a model that legitimately chose to talk instead of generate.

Etch now calls models.generateImages (Imagen, default model imagen-3.0-generate-002) — the endpoint built specifically for image generation. Its response type has no text field at all, so "the model just described the image in prose" becomes structurally impossible rather than merely less likely. The only "declined" shape it can return is a filtered result with an explicit raiFilteredReason, which is still treated as a non-retryable refusal the same way a content-safety block was before.

author: jacob-delgado
body:
Everything coaching writes onto a match was unsearchable. `bareBlob` read the
annotation's note, tags, members and replay code — but not the player's own
timestamped moments, and not the blocks a coach sent back.

So *"that thing the coach said about my off-angles"* came back empty while the
text sat on the match in plain sight. That is the wrong way round for this app:
stats are what you filter by, prose is what you remember a fragment of and go
looking for.

## What the blob now carries

From both directions —

- a player's own moment text
- a coach note's text
- the moments **nested inside** a returned note (the half of a timestamped
  review that points at something)
- the focus and extra tags it was filed under
- the coach's name, so "everything Ordo reviewed" is one search

Scoped clauses are deliberately untouched: `note:` / `tag:` / `member:` /
`replay:` still mean the player's own annotation surfaces. Widening those would
quietly change what an existing saved search means.

## Verification

Unit and e2e, both mutation-verified — drop `coachingWords` from the blob and
three e2e cases plus two unit cases fail. The e2e corpus gained a coached match
whose prose lives in **no other surface**, so a pass cannot come from the map
or the hero name.

## Known gap, deliberately not fixed here

The ⌘K palette — which **Ctrl+F now opens** (#705) — scores rows on
`hero · map` only, so it still will not find this text. Widening it means
either putting prose into the label (which is what the row displays) or scoring
against a haystack the label does not show, which breaks the hit-highlighting
contract that `segments()` relies on.

That is a design call worth making on its own rather than smuggling into this
PR. Flagging it because the Ctrl+F wiring makes the palette look like the place
this should work.

## Summary

- add and enable the Zavetišče Horjul provider
- discover stable WordPress post IDs from the combined adoption catalogue
- parse dogs and cats from detail-page category classes
- normalize labeled sex, numeric intake age, size, intake date, municipality, medical facts, status, and shelter-hosted images

The parser uses the catalogue's stable WordPress post IDs for identity and only maps a found location to `originMunicipality` when the page explicitly labels it as `Občina …`.

For listings such as Klopka, `9 tednov` at intake is converted to approximately two months and aged forward from `25. 7. 2016`; at the verification crawl date this yields 122 months (about 10 years 2 months). Klopka’s live page also verifies 14 shelter-hosted photos across the main carousel and journal galleries, rather than only the single carousel image.

The changing “Pri nas je N dni” counter is not needed for age calculation because the labeled intake date and crawl timestamp provide the stable elapsed duration.
